issues.legal_issue: An unexplained, substantially delayed application to strike a pleading should be assessed in light of the applicant’s earlier acceptance of the pleading and conduct of the proceedings.
material_facts: The additional written statement was filed and taken on record without objection, and additional issues were framed.
The plaintiffs led evidence with knowledge of the additional written statement and completed their evidence before applying to strike it.
The plaintiffs did not explain why they waited to object.
issues.conclusion: The High Court should not have brushed aside the delay; the trial court was justified in dismissing the application to strike the additional written statement.
issues.legal_principle: The effect of delay must be examined in the circumstances of the proceedings, including whether the applicant accepted the pleading, proceeded with the case in light of it, and offered an explanation for the delay. The court also noted that the application itself had delayed the proceedings.

predicates.application_to_strike_a_pleading: A party applied to have another party’s pleading removed from the case.
predicates.pleading_taken_on_record_without_objecti: The challenged pleading was accepted into the case without an objection from the applicant.
predicates.applicant_led_evidence_with_knowledge_of: The applicant presented evidence knowing the contents of the challenged pleading.
predicates.unexplained_substantial_delay: The applicant waited a substantial time to seek removal of the pleading and gave no explanation for waiting.

issues.definition: When a party accepts a pleading, presents evidence knowing its contents, and later seeks its removal after an unexplained substantial delay, the application is rejected.

issues.legal_issue: A court may strike out a pleading only when the pleading falls within a recognized ground for striking pleadings, and that power must be exercised cautiously.
material_facts: The plaintiffs sought to strike the legal representatives’ additional written statement, which raised matters concerning title arising from inventory proceedings.
The trial court found that the plaintiffs had not established a ground for striking the pleading.
The High Court ordered the pleading struck without considering whether a recognized ground for doing so had been established.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was not justified in striking the additional written statement without finding that a ground for striking pleadings had been made out.
issues.legal_principle: Under Order VI Rule 16 of the Code of Civil Procedure, a court may strike or amend matter in a pleading that is unnecessary, scandalous, frivolous, or vexatious; tends to prejudice, embarrass, or delay a fair trial; or is otherwise an abuse of the court’s process. The power is extraordinary and must be used sparingly and with care. The Court relied on Knowles v. Roberts, as approved in Sathi Vijay Kumar v. Tota Singh, and referred to Roop Lal Sathi v. Nachhattar Singh Gill, K.K. Modi v. K.N. Modi, and Union Bank of India v. Naresh Kumar.

predicates.application_to_strike_a_pleading: A party applied to have another party’s pleading removed from the case.
predicates.no_recognized_ground_for_striking_establ: The applicant did not establish that the pleading was improper, unfairly prejudicial, or an abuse of the court’s process.

issues.definition: If a party seeks removal of a pleading but does not establish a recognized ground for doing so, the pleading is not struck.

issues.legal_issue: A High Court exercising review or supervisory jurisdiction over a subordinate court’s interlocutory order cannot act as an appellate court and alter the order without the required jurisdictional or manifest error and resulting injustice.
material_facts: The High Court reviewed the trial court’s refusal to strike the additional written statement.

The High Court treated the matter as if it were hearing an appeal and did not establish that the trial court’s order involved a jurisdictional error, a manifest error of law, or a relevant breach of natural justice.
The High Court did not establish substantial failure of justice or manifest injustice resulting from the trial court’s order.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was not justified in setting aside the trial court’s order and striking the additional written statement.
issues.legal_principle: Under Articles 226 and 227 of the Constitution, certiorari and supervisory jurisdiction are limited and are not substitutes for an appeal. Intervention requires, as applicable, a jurisdictional error, a manifest error apparent on the record, or a procedural or natural-justice defect, together with substantial failure of justice or grave injustice. The Court relied on Syed Yakoob v. K.S. Radhakrishnan and the principles in Surya Dev Rai v. Ram Chander Rai.

predicates.review_of_subordinate_court_interlocutor: A party sought High Court review of an interlocutory order made by a subordinate court.
predicates.no_jurisdictional_or_manifest_error: The challenged order was not shown to contain a jurisdictional error or a manifest error apparent on the record.
predicates.no_substantial_or_grave_injustice: The challenged order was not shown to have caused substantial failure of justice or grave injustice.

issues.definition: When reviewing an interlocutory order, the High Court must not set it aside if no jurisdictional or manifest error and no substantial or grave injustice are shown.

issues.legal_issue: Legal representatives joined to a civil suit may raise an independent title defence in their additional pleading when the court can determine that title and the defence is not inconsistent with the deceased defendant’s position.
material_facts: The deceased defendant had pleaded that the tenant surrendered the premises and that the premises were later occupied with his permission, but had not claimed ownership of the property.
After being joined as legal representatives, the heirs pleaded that the property had been allotted to some of them through inventory proceedings approved by the court.
The plaintiffs did not object when the additional written statement was filed and led evidence with that pleading on record.
The action was before a civil court capable of determining the asserted title.
issues.conclusion: The heirs’ title plea was not inconsistent with the deceased defendant’s defence, and the High Court was not justified in striking the additional written statement on that basis.
issues.legal_principle: Order XXII Rule 4(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure permits a person joined as a legal representative to make a defence appropriate to that capacity. J.C. Chatterjee v. Sri Kishan recognizes that legal representatives may also set up an independent title, subject to the court’s ability to determine it. Bal Kishan v. Om Parkash limits that principle where the forum lacks jurisdiction to decide independent title, and Vidyawati v. Man Mohan distinguishes an independent claim that is not consonant with the deceased defendant’s defence.

predicates.legal_representatives_joined_in_civil_su: Persons were joined in a civil suit as the legal representatives of a deceased defendant.
predicates.court_can_determine_independent_title: The court hearing the suit has authority to decide the independent title asserted by the legal representatives.
predicates.independent_title_defence_not_inconsiste: The legal representatives’ asserted title does not contradict the material defence taken by the deceased defendant.

issues.definition: Legal representatives joined in a civil suit may assert independent title in their defence when the court can determine that title and the assertion does not contradict the deceased defendant’s defence.
